step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject of case presentation; 42-year-old male with acute febrile illness, jaundice, hepatitis relapse

step5_concept_grounding: Wild-type yellow fever virus infection confirmed by RT-PCR during first acute hepatitis episode, presenting with relapsing hepatitis
step9_key_evidence: Positive yellow fever virus RT-PCR (YF-PCR) obtained during initial acute hepatitis presentation
Severe acute hepatitis during urban yellow fever outbreak with AST 2216 U/L, ALT 1611 U/L, total bilirubin 6.36 mg/dL, and thrombocytopenia (52,000/mm3)
Hepatitis relapse 40 days post-discharge with rebound jaundice (total bilirubin 19.2 mg/dL) and transaminitis (ALT 2289 U/L)
rationale: A 42-year-old male presented during a yellow fever outbreak in Brazil with acute febrile hepatitis and jaundice. Yellow fever virus infection was laboratory-confirmed by positive YF-PCR from a blood sample during the acute phase (E1 confirmatory evidence). The patient subsequently developed a late hepatitis relapse 40 days post-discharge. All Valid Positive Diagnosis (VPD) criteria are fully satisfied.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Patient admitted with fever, myalgia, and headache, diagnosed with concurrent DENV2 and YFV coinfection

step5_concept_grounding: Acute Yellow Fever coinfection with Dengue virus serotype 2
step9_key_evidence: Genetic material from Yellow Fever Virus (YFV) detected in patient serum by multiplex qRT-PCR (ABI 7500)
Clinical presentation of acute febrile illness with elevated direct bilirubin, ALT, AST, GGT, and C-reactive protein
rationale: Patient presented with acute arboviral illness and had confirmed Yellow Fever Virus genetic material detected by multiplex qRT-PCR (E1 confirmatory laboratory evidence) alongside DENV-2. Fulfills all Valid Positive Diagnosis criteria as true coinfection -> POSITIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject of case presentation; 13-year-old boy diagnosed with narcolepsy type 1

step5_concept_grounding: Yellow fever mentioned strictly as prophylactic vaccination (Stamaril live attenuated vaccine) discussed as an immunological trigger for narcolepsy
step9_key_evidence: Vaccinated with Stamaril live attenuated yellow fever vaccine approximately 2 weeks prior to symptom onset for a family trip to Africa
No clinical features or laboratory evidence of wild-type yellow fever disease
Confirmed diagnosis of narcolepsy type 1 based on polysomnography, MSLT, and HLA-DQB1*0602 positivity
rationale: The primary clinical subject is a 13-year-old male diagnosed with narcolepsy type 1. Yellow fever appears exclusively as a prior preventive vaccination (Stamaril vaccine) evaluated as a possible autoimmune trigger. The patient never contracted wild-type yellow fever infection. Per protocol rules, prophylactic vaccination context without target disease infection warrants EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 65-year-old male with severe yellow fever presenting with persistent shedding in urine and semen

step5_concept_grounding: Convalescent yellow fever infection with persistent viral RNA shedding in urine and semen
step9_key_evidence: Yellow fever virus RNA detected by real-time quantitative RT-PCR in urine and semen samples
Complete YFV genome sequenced from urine isolate demonstrating South American I genotype
Clinical illness with fever, severe body pain, prostration, jaundice, and dark yellow urine
rationale: A 65-year-old male contracted yellow fever during the Brazilian epidemic. YFV RNA was detected by qRT-PCR and the complete viral genome was sequenced (E1 confirmatory evidence). Fulfills all VPD criteria -> POSITIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 21-year-old female traveler from Angola to Japan evaluated for yellow fever, diagnosed with chikungunya

step5_concept_grounding: Yellow fever evaluated and ruled out by negative RT-PCR in traveler with acute febrile illness from Angola
step9_key_evidence: Real-time reverse transcription PCR for yellow fever virus was explicitly confirmed to be negative
Patient had documented acute Chikungunya virus infection
rationale: A 21-year-old female returned from Angola with acute fever and polyarthralgia. Given an active yellow fever outbreak in Angola, real-time RT-PCR for yellow fever was performed and was negative. Chikungunya was confirmed instead. Target disease ruled out -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject of case presentation; 67-year-old female presenting with status epilepticus and encephalitis

step5_concept_grounding: Yellow fever vaccine-associated neurotropic disease (YEL-AND) resulting from 17D live attenuated vaccine, not wild-type yellow fever virus infection
step9_key_evidence: Received 17D yellow fever vaccine 2 months prior to hospital presentation
Positive serum and CSF YFV IgM with CSF PRNT90 titer 1:256 and serum PRNT90 titer 1:640 confirming vaccine-associated neurotropic disease (YEL-AND)
No evidence of wild-type yellow fever virus infection
rationale: The patient is a 67-year-old female who developed yellow fever vaccine-associated neurotropic disease (YEL-AND) following 17D vaccination, confirmed by CSF YFV IgM and PRNT90 titers. Per project protocol (Step 8 and Step 12), vaccine adverse events are classified under clinical_role PREVENTION_VACCINATION and are explicitly excluded from the target disease gold standard (EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE) because they represent vaccine complications rather than wild-type yellow fever disease.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject of case presentation; 50-year-old female with post-vaccine diffuse uveitis

step5_concept_grounding: Adverse reaction following yellow fever vaccination (systemic reaction and diffuse uveitis), not wild-type yellow fever infection
step9_key_evidence: Administration of single dose of yellow fever vaccine (Biomanguinhos/Fiocruz, lot 160VFA0433)
Development of post-vaccination systemic reaction followed by bilateral asymmetric diffuse uveitis and chorioretinal alterations
No diagnostic evidence of wild-type yellow fever infection
rationale: A 50-year-old woman developed systemic symptoms and bilateral diffuse uveitis following receipt of a yellow fever vaccine. The authors describe this as a vaccine-related adverse event. Under the 12-step protocol, vaccine-associated adverse reactions carry clinical_role PREVENTION_VACCINATION and do not represent wild-type yellow fever, requiring assignment of EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Primary subject of case presentation; 10-month-old female infant with severe combined immunodeficiency

step5_concept_grounding: Yellow fever vaccine-associated viscerotropic and neurotropic disease (YEL-AVD/YEL-AND) caused by 17DD live attenuated vaccine in an infant with SCID
step9_key_evidence: Received 17DD live attenuated yellow fever vaccine 28 days before symptom onset
Positive YFV IgM MAC-ELISA in serum and CSF in the setting of severe vaccine-associated viscerotropic and neurotropic disease
Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) confirmed by absence of TRECs on RT-PCR and severe T-cell lymphopenia
rationale: A 10-month-old infant experienced fatal vaccine-associated viscerotropic and neurotropic disease (YEL-AVD/YEL-AND) after receiving the 17DD live attenuated yellow fever vaccine, which subsequently led to the diagnosis of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). In accordance with protocol specifications, vaccine-associated adverse events are classified under clinical_role PREVENTION_VACCINATION and do not qualify as wild-type yellow fever disease, requiring EXCLUDED_NON_TARGET_CASE.
